Élections municipales – les propositions: Municipal Elections: Proposals from People Experiencing Homelessness
Les personnes itinérantes de Montréal pa: Montréal's homeless population shares what they expect from elected officials to take real action on the housing crisis.
Jean-Christophe, Montréalais vivant l’it: Jean-Christophe, a Montréaler experiencing homelessness, shares his views on the housing and homelessness crisis. Photo credit: Charline Caro
Avec les élections municipales qui appro: With the municipal elections approaching, there is a lot of talk about the homelessness crisis and how to tackle it, whether in candidates' speeches or in the media. But what do people experiencing homelessness think themselves? Since they are absent from the public debate, we wanted to listen to them so they could give their opinion on the situation and explain their needs.
‍<strong>Alors que la campagne en vue de: ‍As the campaign for the municipal elections is in full swing, candidates for mayor of Montréal are presenting their plans to fight the homelessness crisis, which they describe as “urgent” and a “priority.” What do the people affected think?‍
« Merveilleux ! » En arrivant dans la ca: “Wonderful!” Walking into the cafeteria of the Old Brewery Mission, Jean-Christophe is thrilled at the idea of talking about the municipal elections. “I'm going to have a lot to say about this!” he says happily.
Comme pour marquer l’occasion, il porte: As if to mark the occasion, he is wearing a suit jacket over his sweatshirt. He has a big smile in his beard, and his green eyes sparkle with excitement. Coffee in hand, he sits down at the table, apologizing for being a little late.
Jean-Christophe est un Montréalais de 35: Jean-Christophe is a 35-year-old Montréaler who has been homeless since last December, “after a separation.” After being housed for a while by an acquaintance, he arrived in September at the Old Brewery Mission, an organization that supports people who are homeless or at risk of homelessness.
Jean-Christophe enchaîne tout de suite s: Jean-Christophe goes straight into the municipal elections, the main subject of our meeting, for which he prepared the day before. “I'm pretty up to date on all that,” he tells us over the background noise of a coffee machine. “I read the Journal de Montréal and La Presse every day,” he says eagerly, as well as “the candidates' platforms.” Jean-Christophe keeps informed out of interest, but also to find out what the candidates for mayor of Montréal are proposing to deal with the homelessness crisis.
Pour lui, les responsables politiques n’: In his view, politicians are not doing enough about what he considers a “huge crisis.” “Where are the actions?” he asks, throwing his hands in the air. “They say they've invested money, but where did they put it? The situation is still just as bad,” he laments. Jean-Christophe has high expectations of the would-be mayors and hopes they will put homelessness at the top of their “list of priorities.”
« Je n’ai pas l’impression que les candi: “I don't feel like the candidates are really talking about homelessness, they're too busy bickering on Facebook,” says Vicky angrily. We meet her in her apartment in Saint-Henri. She welcomes us dressed all in beige and wearing large glasses, behind which we can see her blue eyes. A mother of four, she was homeless for “three intense years” and struggled with drug addiction.
Elle vit aujourd’hui avec son jeune fils: She now lives with her young son in social housing and works as a cook at a college. Sitting on her couch, she keeps one eye on her son playing in the living room while reflecting on the homelessness situation in Montréal and what she expects from the elections.
« Quelque chose dont on a absolument bes: “Something we absolutely need is housing,” says Jean-Christophe with a grave look. “You can want to get homeless people off the street all you like, but if there's no housing, where's the solution?” he exclaims.
Pour les personnes rencontrées, les budg: For the people we met, the budgets allocated to homelessness should be invested first and foremost in transitional and social housing. “For me, that's what helped,” says Vicky, who spent several years in transitional housing, long enough to “take care of [her] mental health,” “work on [her] addiction” and “start the process of finding a job.” In her view, transitional housing is essential to “find the time to look for resources.”
Il y a aussi les logements sociaux, rapp: Then there is social housing, she adds, particularly for low-income people or those coming out of homelessness. “It's not true that people on minimum wage get by,” she insists, especially in a context where “housing in Montréal is very expensive.”
La place des personnes itinérantes dans: The place of homeless people in public space is sometimes called into question in political and media discourse that puts the safety and tranquility of residents front and centre. Last spring, the Société de transport de Montréal (STM) banned loitering in the metro to ease users' growing sense of insecurity.
Pour Vicky, il faut « laisser faire » le: For Vicky, people who are homeless should be “left alone,” since they are “adults and vaccinated.” She admits, however, that some behaviours are not safe, especially when it comes to drug use. “I encourage my son to say hello to homeless people, but I don't want him to see situations involving drugs,” she says. She adds that, personally, being confronted with scenes of drug use on the street “puts [her] sobriety at risk.”
Jean-Christophe estime pour sa part que: Jean-Christophe, for his part, believes homeless people are “not dangerous at all,” even though some may go through crises. “You know, they're human beings like everybody else,” he reminds us. As for residents who want to preserve their “tranquility,” Jean-Christophe believes the solution is to offer resources to homeless people rather than “just shoving them out of these neighbourhoods.”
Les candidats à la mairie de Montréal co: Candidates for mayor of Montréal describe the homelessness crisis sometimes as a “priority,” sometimes as an “emergency.” What are they proposing to address it?
Projet Montréal – et son candidat à la m: Projet Montréal, and its mayoral candidate Luc Rabouin, wants to set up 500 modular units and 500 transitional housing units for people in vulnerable situations. The party also intends to double funding for community organizations working on homelessness.
Ensemble Montréal – le parti de Soraya M: Ensemble Montréal, Soraya Martinez Ferrada's party, promises to develop 2,000 transitional and permanent housing units, in addition to creating “small shelters” throughout the city. The budget for fighting homelessness would then be tripled, amounting to $30 million per year. The party also wants to end the presence of tents on Montréal's streets and ensure “harmonious” and “safe” coexistence between homeless people and neighbouring residents.
Transition Montréal – le parti de Craig: Transition Montréal, Craig Sauvé's party, for its part pledges to declare a state of emergency in order to requisition hotels and vacant buildings to offer temporary shelter to people experiencing homelessness during the winter. The party also wants to ban the dismantling of encampments and police access to these sites, while setting up community and social services there. Finally, the Sauvé administration would triple funding for community organizations working on homelessness.
Action Montréal – parti mené par Gilbert: Action Montréal, a party led by Gilbert Thibodeau, proposes better coordination among organizations and using places of worship as temporary shelters.
« S’ils respectent vraiment leurs progra: “If they really stick to their programs, maybe we'll start to see the light at the end of the tunnel,” says Jean-Christophe hopefully. He finds several proposals “interesting,” such as investing $30 million a year in the fight against homelessness. On the condition that “the money goes to the right place,” warns the man in his thirties.
Vicky accueille favorablement la proposi: Vicky welcomes the proposal not to dismantle encampments. “I'd say they should be tolerated rather than encouraged,” she qualifies, adding that support resources must be developed alongside.
Au-delà des programmes, Vicky et Jean-Ch: Beyond the platforms, Vicky and Jean-Christophe stress the importance of listening to the people affected. “It's good to talk about homelessness, but it's also important to talk with homeless people,” pleads the Old Brewery Mission resident. “Invite them to your city council and listen to their ideas,” he suggests to future elected officials, who will only then be able to grasp “the real issues.”
« Je pense que les solutions, ça vient d: “I think the solutions come from us,” says Vicky, who would like to share her many suggestions with municipal elected officials.
Avant de logement, nuance Vicky, les per: Before housing, Vicky qualifies, people experiencing homelessness “need care.” The mother argues for better access to mental health and addiction services, an essential step in her view to “get off the street.” “It's been five years since I last used,” she tells us, a hint of pride in her voice. But the road to sobriety was hard, and still is, she explains.
Alors que le démantèlement des campement: While the dismantling of homeless encampments regularly fuels political debate, Jean-Christophe believes it is not the main issue. What matters, he says, is the support offered outside these encampments. “If you send these people into housing without dealing with their addiction problems, there's a 50% chance they'll end up back in an encampment soon,” he says. Politicians must take into account how long the process of getting off the street takes, Jean-Christophe maintains. They must, therefore, put “the money into the necessary resources.”
Au-delà de l’accompagnement disponible,: Beyond the support available, Vicky points out that you can't force someone out of homelessness. “If the person doesn't have the will, it won't work,” she says. “I got off the street and off drugs several times before going back, because I wasn't mentally ready.”
Face aux discours qui veulent résoudre à: Faced with discourse that wants to solve the homelessness crisis at all costs, Vicky adds a caveat: “We'd like everyone to make it out, but it's not always possible. I know that what I'm saying is plate.”
Dans tous les cas, le prochain maire ou: Either way, Montréal's next mayor “will have a hell of a job to do!” exclaims Vicky. Even though she has not yet seen any “politicians who really made a change,” she hopes the “new faces” in municipal politics will make a difference in the fight against the homelessness crisis. “That's how I am in life, I always try to believe in someone,” she adds with a smile.
« Si je pouvais m’adresser aux candidats: “If I could speak to the candidates, I'd ask them to keep their election promises,” says Jean-Christophe. “Over four years, if you invest as much as you promise, it can definitely change something.”
